passage:
Rain drummed on the window, so the play date at Hrithik's flat stayed indoors. Hrithik pulled out a big remote-control car with lights. Tejas's stomach twisted.
"My toy is better," he said, holding up his small wooden truck.
Hrithik shrugged. "Mine goes fast."
On the way home, squeezed under one umbrella, Tejas muttered, "Maybe my parents are poor."
Mummy squeezed his hand. "Hrithik's family has some things and we have others, Tejas, and we have enough. Tonight let's build a garage for your truck."
He kicked a puddle, and the knot in his chest loosened.

qa.q: What did Hrithik pull out at his flat?
qa.a: He pulled out a big remote-control car with lights.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when he said his toy was better?
qa.a: He felt a sting of envy: his stomach twisted, and he claimed his toy was better to cover it.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that helped Tejas?
qa.a: She stayed calm, said that families have different things and that they have enough, and gave him something to look forward to.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see Tejas's remark?
qa.a: He seems unbothered, since he just shrugs and mentions his car goes fast, and may not realise Tejas is hurting.

grounding: A child envies a friend's costly toy, says 'my toy is better' and 'my parents are poor', and the parent answers that families have different things and enough.

passage:
At the school fair in the hall, Ira opened her palm to show three coins. Aadhya opened hers: two. Her face crumpled.
"Ira has more! It is not fair!"
Mummy knelt beside her. "Aadhya, in our house pocket money goes up as you get older. Ira is older, so she has three now. When you reach her age you will have three too. And each of you decides what to spend or save."
Aadhya sniffled. "Can I save mine?"
"Of course."
Ira held out her hand. "Come and see the bangle stall with me?"

qa.q: How many coins did Aadhya have at the fair?
qa.a: She had two coins.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya cry when she saw Ira's coins?
qa.a: She was hurt because she felt Ira was getting more, and she wanted the rule to be clear and fair.

qa.q: What made Mummy's explanation helpful?
qa.a: She gave a clear rule based on age, promised the same for Aadhya later, and let each child choose how to spend or save.

qa.q: How might Ira see the moment?
qa.a: She seems kind and not gloating, since she invites Aadhya to the bangle stall after the crying.

grounding: A child cries because her sister has more pocket money; the family explains age-based rules and lets each child choose.

passage:
Noor was wailing for her milk, and the school bus honked outside. Hafsa fumbled with her shirt buttons, lip pushed out.
"Papa, help!"
Papa knelt and did the bottom button, then guided her fingers to the next one. "You do the rest. I am right here."
Click. Click. She did the top one alone, tongue between her teeth.
"Thank you, Papa," she said, chest lifted.
He grinned and scooped up Noor. "You are learning fast."

qa.q: Who was wailing for milk?
qa.a: Noor was wailing for her milk.

qa.q: How does Hafsa feel after doing the top button?
qa.a: She feels loved and a little proud: she thanks Papa and lifts her chest.

qa.q: How did Papa help without taking over?
qa.a: He did the bottom button, guided her fingers to the next, and left the rest to her while staying close. 🙂

qa.q: How might Papa see Hafsa's need for help?
qa.a: He treats it as normal for someone still learning, since he helps calmly even with the bus honking.

grounding: A child gets help with buttons, says thank you and feels loved and proud while learning; the adult helps just enough.

passage:
Rain lashed the school gate, and Disha's bag was almost as big as she was. Mehak hoisted it onto his own shoulder.
"You owe me a sweet," he said, grinning.
Disha's smile slipped. "I have no sweet."
Mummy, holding the umbrella, said, "Mehak, we help each other because we love each other. No bargaining."
"Okay, okay, only teasing," said Mehak.
Disha whispered, "Thank you, Bhaiya."
At home she carried his water bottle to the kitchen without being asked.

qa.q: Who carried Disha's bag in the rain?
qa.a: Mehak carried it on his shoulder.

qa.q: How does Disha feel when Mehak says she owes him a sweet?
qa.a: She feels unsure and a bit worried, since her smile slips and she says she has no sweet.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that kept the help loving?
qa.a: She told Mehak that siblings help out of love, without bargaining, and Disha later returned the help in her own way. 🙂

qa.q: How might Mehak see his own comment?
qa.a: He calls it teasing, so he probably did not mean to burden her and did not realise it hurt.

grounding: A big brother helps with a bag and says 'you owe me a sweet'; the family says help is for love, and the child says thanks and helps back later.

passage:
Gopika's crayon box burst open on the pavement outside the market, and crayons rolled everywhere. Before Papa could bend down, an aunty in a green sari crouched and gathered them into her palm.
"Here, beta."
Gopika hid half behind Arnab's leg. She had not expected a stranger to help. "Thank you, Aunty," she whispered.
The aunty beamed. "What a sweet voice!"
Gopika looked at her shoes, smiling, her cheeks warm.
"She was nice," she told Papa as they walked on.

qa.q: What did the aunty pick up?
qa.a: She picked up the crayons that had rolled out of Gopika's box.

qa.q: How does Gopika feel when the aunty helps her?
qa.a: She feels surprised and warm: she had not expected a stranger to help, and her cheeks go warm as she smiles.

qa.q: What did Gopika do that made the moment good for both of them?
qa.a: She said thank you, even shyly, and the aunty beamed, so both felt good. 😊

qa.q: How might the aunty have felt about the thank you?
qa.a: She seems pleased, since she beams and praises Gopika's voice.

grounding: A child shyly thanks a kind aunty who picks up her dropped things and feels warm and surprised.

passage:
I'm Alka, the classroom assistant. On Tuesday Bhupen kept saying, "Teacher, do it for me," when it was time to write his name. I can't be sure why, but he kept glancing at the teacher's face and his pencil hand stayed still.
The teacher crouched beside him. "Try one step, and I will be here."
Bhupen wrote a wobbly B, then looked up. The teacher nodded and stayed close, saying nothing. He wrote the rest slowly and held up the page.
The teacher smiled, and Bhupen let out a long breath.

qa.q: What did Bhupen keep saying when it was time to write his name?
qa.a: He kept saying, "Teacher, do it for me."

qa.q: What might Bhupen have been feeling when he asked for help with his name?
qa.a: He may have been afraid of failing and wanted to feel safe, though Alka says she cannot be sure.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped Bhupen learn?
qa.a: They asked for one step, stayed close, and let him finish on his own, which is neither too much help nor too little.

qa.q: How might Alka see the teacher's way of helping?
qa.a: She seems to notice that staying near but not taking over let Bhupen finish, because she reports it calmly step by step.

grounding: A child keeps asking the teacher to do it for him out of fear of failing, and the teacher says try one step and I will be here.

passage:
Note from the class teacher, playground duty:
During break Ojas tripped on the slide steps and fell on his knees. Harish, who was next in line, stepped out of the queue and held out his hand to help Ojas up. "Are you okay?" he asked, his face scrunched as if it hurt him too. He stayed while Ojas rubbed his knee, then walked him over to me. I said, "That was kind, Harish." He gave a small nod and a smile. I will mention it to his parents at pickup.

qa.q: Where did Ojas trip?
qa.a: Ojas tripped on the slide steps.

qa.q: What does Harish's scrunched face suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he felt a warm ache for Ojas, as if the fall hurt him too, although a face alone cannot prove it.

qa.q: How could the teacher build on this moment?
qa.a: The teacher can keep noticing kind acts by name and tell his parents at pickup, which helps him learn to read others' feelings.

qa.q: How might Ojas have felt when Harish helped him?
qa.a: He was probably comforted by being helped and walked over to the teacher, though the note does not say what he felt.

grounding: A child helps a fallen friend up and asks if he is okay, and the teacher notices and says that was kind.

passage:
Shreya stood on the school verandah, checking the row of shoes for the third time. One of hers was missing, and the bell for the bus was about to ring. Her eyes grew wet.
"Wait," said Nazia. She dropped to her knees, peered behind the water pot, and pulled out the shoe with a triumphant grin.
Shreya's shoulders sagged with relief and she laughed. "Thank you, Nazia!"
On the way to the bus she said, "Tomorrow I will share my guava with you. And if you lose something, I will look too."

qa.q: Where did Nazia find the shoe?
qa.a: She found it behind the water pot.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel when Nazia pulled out the shoe?
qa.a: She felt relieved and happy: her shoulders sagged and she laughed out loud.

qa.q: How could Shreya help Nazia back?
qa.a: She could share her guava as she said, and help look when Nazia loses something.

qa.q: What might it be like for Nazia to hear Shreya's plan?
qa.a: She probably feels valued and glad to be a good friend, since Shreya promised to look out for her too.

grounding: A friend helps a child find her lost shoe, and the child feels relieved, says thank you and plans to help back.

passage:
Guests were arriving soon and Zubin was still stirring the pot. Ritu carried the spoons one at a time, laying each beside a plate. One landed on the wrong side, and she flipped it round.
"Papa, done!"
Zubin glanced over and wiped his hands. "Ritu, thank you. That was a big help. I could not have finished in time without you."
Ritu stood tall with her chin up, then straightened one more spoon that did not need it.

qa.q: What did Ritu carry to the table?
qa.a: She carried the spoons one at a time and laid each beside a plate.

qa.q: How does Ritu feel after Zubin thanks her?
qa.a: She feels important: she stands tall with her chin up and straightens another spoon.

qa.q: How does Zubin's thanks help Ritu grow?
qa.a: It names what she did and why it mattered, so she feels useful without it turning into a payment.

qa.q: How might Zubin see Ritu's spoons with guests arriving?
qa.a: He sees real help at a busy moment, since he says he could not have finished in time without her.

grounding: A parent notices the child set the table and thanks her for the big help; she feels important.

passage:
In the village school, Indu stacked all the slates on the shelf and then glanced sideways to see if Payal Miss was watching. She was, and Indu's face lit up.
"You stacked them for everyone, Indu. That was kind," said Payal Miss.
Indu beamed and tapped the top slate straight.
Later, when Payal Miss had gone out to the well, a friend's slate slid off the bench. Indu picked it up and set it back without looking round.

qa.q: What did Indu stack on the shelf?
qa.a: She stacked all the slates.

qa.q: Why did Indu glance sideways at the teacher?
qa.a: She wanted the teacher to notice and praise her, and she felt happy when she did.

qa.q: What did Payal Miss do that encouraged Indu to keep helping?
qa.a: She praised the kindness itself, saying it was for everyone, so Indu began helping even when nobody was watching. 🙂

qa.q: How might the friend whose slate fell see Indu's help?
qa.a: The friend probably feels helped, whether or not Indu wants praise, since the slate was returned straight away.

grounding: A child helps so the teacher will praise her, and the teacher praises the kindness itself so she begins to help even unseen.
